claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain before failure than commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater toughness than commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
The multiple principal refractory elements in WTaTiVZr produce severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion creates a heterogeneous energy landscape that impedes abrupt dislocation motion.
Distributed dislocation activation and strain hardening delay crack nucleation and propagation.
Pure tungsten has a relatively brittle dislocation response under the relevant conditions.
The tested WTaTiVZr material can be prepared as a single-phase, homogeneous, fine-grained BCC alloy.
Matching grain size, defect density, and processing history between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten provides a controlled comparison intended to isolate the compositional mechanism.
Mechanical testing at 800–1000 °C is relevant to plasma-facing-component service.
WTaTiVZr is composed of reduced-activity refractory metals suitable for consideration in nuclear-reactor environments.
Heterogeneous local stress fields in WTaTiVZr act as distributed obstacles and promote dislocation entanglement.
Dislocation entanglement in WTaTiVZr produces continuous strain hardening.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder increases the variation in local barriers for dislocation activation.
A dispersed distribution of activation barriers produces more uniform and controlled dislocation glide.
More uniform dislocation glide delays localized damage and thereby increases ductility and toughness.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than pure tungsten under identical high-temperature loading.
The proposed mechanism is applicable specifically at 800–1000 °C when grain sizes and defect densities are comparable.
The magnitude of the proposed toughness and ductility improvement is uncertain because of microstructural variability and complex high-temperature dislocation dynamics.
Dislocation density and activation-volume measurements can be used to test whether WTaTiVZr has more heterogeneous dislocation dynamics than pure tungsten.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement of more than approximately 10–15% in both plastic strain and toughness, or failure to observe distinct dislocation dynamics, would falsify the hypothesis.
